metadata.narrative: I am an 18 year old that currently has ten thousand dollars. Write an investment plan to guide me through investing for the future. Specifically, the timespan of this investment plan should be considered to be the rest of my life. Furthermore, this investment plan should be researched with academic and/or authoritative sources. Essentially, I want to understand how a savvy investor would invest, given that they are starting with ten thousand dollars at the age of 18.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: A savvy 18-year-old with $10,000 has one advantage no skill can replicate later: time, and the first move is not investing at all but securing the foundation.

Financial planners generally recommend building an emergency fund of three to six months of living expenses, creating a budget, and paying off high-interest debt before committing money to markets, since money needed within five years should stay in cash rather than stocks.
Once that foundation exists, the most powerful lever available is starting now, because compound growth rewards time above almost everything else.
A hypothetical investor who contributes for only 10 years starting immediately can end up with more money after 30 years than one who waits 10 years and then contributes for twice as long.
A comparison of an investor starting at 22 versus 40 found the early starter finished with roughly 2.88 times more wealth, using the S&P 500's historical average annual return of about 9.8 percent.
This matters because average retirees spend around $46,000 per year while the average Social Security benefit is under $17,000 annually, so investing beyond Social Security is essential.
The order in which money is deployed matters, prioritizing tax-advantaged accounts first.

If a future employer offers a 401(k) match, that should be captured first since it is effectively free money; the average match is about 5.1 percent of pay, and employers also receive tax benefits for offering it.

A Roth IRA is attractive for a young earner because contributions are taxed now while income is low, growth and qualified withdrawals are tax-free, and unlike traditional IRAs there is no required minimum distribution age and no age limit on contributing.
In 2024 the IRS allows up to $7,000 in IRA or Roth IRA contributions per year and up to $23,000 in a 401(k) or similar workplace plan, figures that are periodically raised.
A Health Savings Account, if eligible, adds a further tax-free contribution, growth, and withdrawal vehicle whose unused funds can also be invested rather than left as cash.
For the investment vehicle itself, decades of research favor low-cost, broadly diversified index funds over active stock-picking.

Morningstar found only about 11 percent of large-cap active managers beat their passive benchmark over a 10-year period, and researcher Larry Swedroe found the share of managers generating statistically significant outperformance fell from 20 percent in 1998 to roughly 2 percent by 2020, dropping closer to 1 percent after taxes.
JPMorgan data covering 2002-2021 found the S&P 500 returned an annualized 9.5 percent while the average investor earned only 3.6 percent, a gap driven largely by mistimed buying and selling.

Even Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, despite beating the S&P 500 by nearly 5 percent annually over 27 years, underperformed the index in 8 of those years, showing that even elite active management requires enduring long stretches most investors cannot tolerate.

Cost compounds just as returns do: Vanguard's average fund expense ratio was about 0.10 percent versus an industry average of 0.45 percent, and a total stock market index fund can cost as little as 0.04 percent versus 1 percent or more for many actively managed funds.

On deploying the $10,000 itself, Vanguard research covering 1976-2022 found lump-sum investing outperformed dollar-cost averaging about 68 percent of the time, with the advantage reaching roughly 2.2 percent more annual wealth for all-equity portfolios, though dollar-cost averaging limited losses in the worst-performing years.

This suggests that for an 18-year-old's decades-long horizon, investing the $10,000 promptly in a diversified index fund is statistically favored, while future paycheck contributions will naturally follow a dollar-cost-averaging pattern anyway.

On asset allocation, one reasonable approach is a "total market" portfolio split across a total US stock index, a total US bond index, and a total international stock index, holding at least 20 percent and up to about 55 percent of stock exposure internationally for diversification.

Investors seeking higher expected returns can tilt modestly toward historically higher-returning but riskier segments such as small-cap value or emerging markets, while keeping most of the portfolio in broad market funds.

Given decades until retirement, an 18-year-old can reasonably hold a stock-heavy allocation similar to Vanguard's target-date design for investors more than 25 years from retirement, about 90 percent stocks and 10 percent bonds, though there is no single settled glide path, as shown by rules like "hold your age in bonds" and researcher Wade Pfau's argument for rising equity exposure through retirement.

Over a multi-decade horizon, US stocks have historically outpaced bonds enormously: $100 invested in the S&P 500 in 1928 would have grown to roughly $502,000 by 2019, versus about $48,700 in corporate bonds and just over $8,000 in Treasury bonds.

The long-run average annual return has been about 10 percent since 1926, but that average is nearly meaningless in any single year, since returns landed within two percentage points of it in only 6 of 91 calendar years, underscoring that discipline matters more than prediction.
That discipline is the hardest part, because behavioral research shows investors routinely sabotage their own returns.

Nobel laureates Daniel Kahneman and Richard Thaler documented biases such as fear, greed, and overconfidence that cost the average investor an estimated 1 to 4 percent in returns annually, a pattern visible again during the COVID-19 crash and rebound of 2020.

An MIT study of over 650,000 brokerage accounts found self-described skilled investors were more likely to panic-sell during downturns, and nearly a third of those who panic-sold still had not re-entered the market years later, missing the recovery.

Finally, decades from now, the plan must shift from accumulation to spending, and the widely cited Trinity Study found that withdrawing 3-4 percent of a stock-and-bond portfolio in the first retirement year, then adjusting for inflation, historically sustained a 30-year retirement in nearly all backtested periods from 1925-1995.

Put together, the evidence points toward a simple sequence: secure an emergency cushion, capture any employer match, prioritize a Roth IRA and HSA, invest the lump sum promptly into low-cost diversified index funds with a stock-heavy allocation, keep contributing consistently over a career, avoid emotional trading during crashes, and eventually transition toward a modest, inflation-adjusted withdrawal rate in retirement.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

k.description: Number of fused passages to return (default 10).

I now have comprehensive, well-sourced evidence covering every stage of a lifelong investment plan for an 18-year-old starting with $10,000, so I will write the final report.

A savvy 18-year-old with $10,000 has one enormous advantage that no amount of skill can replicate later: time, and the first move is not investing at all but making sure the foundation is solid.

Financial planners generally recommend building a fully-funded emergency fund of three to six months of living expenses, creating a budget, and paying off any high-interest consumer debt before committing money to markets, since money needed within five years should not be treated as long-term investment capital. [shard_04617_56212]
If part of the $10,000 is earmarked for a near-term need such as a car repair or short-term goal, that portion should sit in cash rather than in stocks. [shard_04617_56212]

Once that foundation exists, the single most powerful lever available to an 18-year-old is simply starting now, because compound growth rewards time above almost everything else.
A hypothetical comparison shows an investor who contributes for only 10 years starting immediately can end up with more money after 30 years than an investor who waits 10 years and then contributes for twice as long. [shard_03589_8024]
A similar comparison of an investor starting at 22 versus one starting at 40 found the early starter finished with roughly 2.88 times more wealth, using the S&P 500's historical average annual return of about 9.8 percent. [shard_02485_63891]
This matters because Social Security alone is unlikely to cover retirement, since average retirees spend around $46,000 per year while the average Social Security benefit is under $17,000 annually. [shard_03589_8024]

The order in which the money is deployed also matters, and the standard sequence prioritizes tax-advantaged accounts first.
If a future employer offers a 401(k) match, that should be captured first because it is effectively free money; the IRS does not require employers to match contributions, but the average match is about 5.1 percent of pay, and employers also receive tax benefits for offering it. [shard_02000_41192]
For a young earner, a Roth IRA is particularly attractive because contributions are taxed now while income is low, growth and qualified withdrawals are tax-free, and unlike traditional IRAs there is no required minimum distribution age and no age limit on contributing as long as earned income exists. [shard_05695_80629]
In 2024 the IRS allows up to $7,000 in IRA or Roth IRA contributions per year and up to $23,000 in a 401(k), 403(b), or similar workplace plan, figures worth revisiting yearly since they are periodically raised. [shard_01177_13296]
A Health Savings Account, if eligible through a high-deductible health plan, offers a rare triple tax advantage: tax-free contributions, tax-free growth, and tax-free withdrawals for medical expenses, and unused HSA funds can be invested in stocks, bonds, or mutual funds rather than left as idle cash. [shard_00100_47340]

For the actual investment vehicle, decades of academic and industry research favor low-cost, broadly diversified index funds over active stock-picking.
Morningstar found that only about 11 percent of large-cap active managers beat their passive benchmark over a 10-year period, and researcher Larry Swedroe found the share of managers generating statistically significant outperformance fell from 20 percent in 1998 to roughly 2 percent by 2020, dropping closer to 1 percent after taxes. [shard_01650_27930]
JPMorgan data covering 2002-2021 found the S&P 500 returned an annualized 9.5 percent while the average investor earned only 3.6 percent, a gap driven largely by mistimed buying and selling rather than fund selection itself. [shard_01650_27930]
Even Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, despite beating the S&P 500 by nearly 5 percent annually over 27 years, underperformed the index in 8 of those years, illustrating that even elite active management requires enduring long stretches of relative underperformance that most investors cannot emotionally tolerate. [shard_02243_67927]
Cost compounds just as returns do: Vanguard's average fund expense ratio was about 0.10 percent versus an industry average of 0.45 percent, and a total stock market index fund can cost as little as 0.04 percent versus 1 percent or more for many actively managed funds. [shard_01268_27033]

On the specific question of how to put the $10,000 to work right away, Vanguard research covering 1976-2022 found that investing a lump sum outperformed dollar-cost averaging about 68 percent of the time, with the advantage growing to roughly 2.2 percent more annual wealth for all-equity portfolios, though dollar-cost averaging did better during the worst-performing years by limiting drawdowns. [shard_01949_40793]
This suggests that for someone with an 18-year-old's decades-long horizon, investing the $10,000 promptly in a diversified index fund is statistically favored over drip-feeding it in, while future paycheck contributions naturally follow a dollar-cost-averaging pattern anyway.

On asset allocation, one reasonable, low-maintenance approach is a "total market" portfolio split roughly evenly across a total US stock index, a total US bond index, and a total international stock index, with recommendations to hold at least 20 percent and up to about 55 percent of stock exposure in international markets for diversification. [shard_01637_54133]
Investors seeking higher expected long-run returns can tilt modestly toward historically higher-returning but riskier segments such as small-cap value or emerging markets, while keeping most of the portfolio in broad market funds. [shard_01637_54133]
Given decades until retirement, an 18-year-old can reasonably hold a stock-heavy allocation similar to Vanguard's target-date design for investors more than 25 years from retirement, which allocates about 90 percent stocks and 10 percent bonds, though popularized rules of thumb like "hold your age in bonds" and researcher Wade Pfau's argument for even rising equity exposure through retirement show there is no single scientifically settled glide path. [shard_06377_4820]

Over a multi-decade horizon, US stocks have historically outpaced bonds by an enormous margin: $100 invested in the S&P 500 in 1928 would have grown to roughly $502,000 by 2019, versus about $48,700 in corporate bonds and just over $8,000 in Treasury bonds. [shard_03490_11965]
The long-run average annual return has been about 10 percent since 1926, but that average is nearly meaningless in any single year, since returns landed within two percentage points of that average in only 6 of 91 calendar years, underscoring that discipline matters more than prediction. [shard_05530_11539]

That discipline is the hardest part, because behavioral research shows investors routinely sabotage their own returns.
Nobel laureates Daniel Kahneman and Richard Thaler have documented behavioral biases such as fear, greed, and overconfidence that cost the average investor an estimated 1 to 4 percent in returns annually, a pattern visible again during the rapid COVID-19 crash and rebound of 2020. [shard_01363_84767]
An MIT study of over 650,000 brokerage accounts found that self-described skilled investors were more likely to panic-sell during downturns, and nearly 31 percent of those who panic-sold had still not re-entered the market years later, missing the eventual recovery. [shard_03178_15386]

Finally, decades from now, the "rest of your life" plan must eventually shift from accumulation to spending, and the widely cited Trinity Study found that withdrawing 3-4 percent of a stock-and-bond portfolio in the first retirement year, then adjusting for inflation, historically sustained a 30-year retirement in nearly all backtested periods from 1925-1995, though economists such as Laurence Kotlikoff have criticized the rule for ignoring how spending should flex with actual portfolio performance. [shard_03504_46021]
Put together, the evidence points toward a simple sequence for an 18-year-old with $10,000: secure an emergency cushion, capture any employer match, prioritize a Roth IRA and HSA, invest the lump sum promptly into low-cost diversified index funds with a stock-heavy allocation, keep contributing consistently over a career, avoid emotional trading during crashes, and eventually transition toward a modest, inflation-adjusted withdrawal rate in retirement.

If a future employer offers a 401(k) match, that should be captured first since it is effectively free money; the average match is about 5.1 percent of pay, and employers also receive tax benefits for offering it.

A Roth IRA is attractive for a young earner because contributions are taxed now while income is low, growth and qualified withdrawals are tax-free, and unlike traditional IRAs there is no required minimum distribution age and no age limit on contributing.
In 2024 the IRS allows up to $7,000 in IRA or Roth IRA contributions per year and up to $23,000 in a 401(k) or similar workplace plan, figures that are periodically raised.
A Health Savings Account, if eligible, adds a further tax-free contribution, growth, and withdrawal vehicle whose unused funds can also be invested rather than left as cash.
For the investment vehicle itself, decades of research favor low-cost, broadly diversified index funds over active stock-picking.

Morningstar found only about 11 percent of large-cap active managers beat their passive benchmark over a 10-year period, and researcher Larry Swedroe found the share of managers generating statistically significant outperformance fell from 20 percent in 1998 to roughly 2 percent by 2020, dropping closer to 1 percent after taxes.
JPMorgan data covering 2002-2021 found the S&P 500 returned an annualized 9.5 percent while the average investor earned only 3.6 percent, a gap driven largely by mistimed buying and selling.

Even Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, despite beating the S&P 500 by nearly 5 percent annually over 27 years, underperformed the index in 8 of those years, showing that even elite active management requires enduring long stretches most investors cannot tolerate.

Cost compounds just as returns do: Vanguard's average fund expense ratio was about 0.10 percent versus an industry average of 0.45 percent, and a total stock market index fund can cost as little as 0.04 percent versus 1 percent or more for many actively managed funds.

On deploying the $10,000 itself, Vanguard research covering 1976-2022 found lump-sum investing outperformed dollar-cost averaging about 68 percent of the time, with the advantage reaching roughly 2.2 percent more annual wealth for all-equity portfolios, though dollar-cost averaging limited losses in the worst-performing years.

This suggests that for an 18-year-old's decades-long horizon, investing the $10,000 promptly in a diversified index fund is statistically favored, while future paycheck contributions will naturally follow a dollar-cost-averaging pattern anyway.

On asset allocation, one reasonable approach is a "total market" portfolio split across a total US stock index, a total US bond index, and a total international stock index, holding at least 20 percent and up to about 55 percent of stock exposure internationally for diversification.

Investors seeking higher expected returns can tilt modestly toward historically higher-returning but riskier segments such as small-cap value or emerging markets, while keeping most of the portfolio in broad market funds.

Given decades until retirement, an 18-year-old can reasonably hold a stock-heavy allocation similar to Vanguard's target-date design for investors more than 25 years from retirement, about 90 percent stocks and 10 percent bonds, though there is no single settled glide path, as shown by rules like "hold your age in bonds" and researcher Wade Pfau's argument for rising equity exposure through retirement.

Over a multi-decade horizon, US stocks have historically outpaced bonds enormously: $100 invested in the S&P 500 in 1928 would have grown to roughly $502,000 by 2019, versus about $48,700 in corporate bonds and just over $8,000 in Treasury bonds.

The long-run average annual return has been about 10 percent since 1926, but that average is nearly meaningless in any single year, since returns landed within two percentage points of it in only 6 of 91 calendar years, underscoring that discipline matters more than prediction.
That discipline is the hardest part, because behavioral research shows investors routinely sabotage their own returns.

Nobel laureates Daniel Kahneman and Richard Thaler documented biases such as fear, greed, and overconfidence that cost the average investor an estimated 1 to 4 percent in returns annually, a pattern visible again during the COVID-19 crash and rebound of 2020.

An MIT study of over 650,000 brokerage accounts found self-described skilled investors were more likely to panic-sell during downturns, and nearly a third of those who panic-sold still had not re-entered the market years later, missing the recovery.

Finally, decades from now, the plan must shift from accumulation to spending, and the widely cited Trinity Study found that withdrawing 3-4 percent of a stock-and-bond portfolio in the first retirement year, then adjusting for inflation, historically sustained a 30-year retirement in nearly all backtested periods from 1925-1995.

Put together, the evidence points toward a simple sequence: secure an emergency cushion, capture any employer match, prioritize a Roth IRA and HSA, invest the lump sum promptly into low-cost diversified index funds with a stock-heavy allocation, keep contributing consistently over a career, avoid emotional trading during crashes, and eventually transition toward a modest, inflation-adjusted withdrawal rate in retirement.
